Fit leakage-safe preprocessing pipeline

Source: R/guards.R
guard_fit.Rd

Builds and fits a guarded preprocessing pipeline on training data, then constructs a transformer for consistent application to new data.

Usage

guard_fit(
  X,
  y = NULL,
  steps = list(),
  task = c("binomial", "multiclass", "gaussian", "survival")
)

Arguments

X

matrix/data.frame of predictors (training).

y

Optional outcome for supervised feature selection.

steps

List of configuration options (see Details).

task

"binomial", "multiclass", "gaussian", or "survival".

Value

An object of class "GuardFit" with elements `transform`, `state`, `p_out`, and `steps`.

Details

The pipeline applies, in order:

  • Winsorization (optional) to limit outliers.

  • Imputation learned on training data only. The requested method is fitted even when the training rows have no missing values, so missing values in new rows are still imputed (for "missForest" with the training medians, as no per-column model exists then).

  • Normalization ("zscore", "robust", frozen reference "quantile", "log_cpm", "clr", or "none").

  • Optional frozen train-only batch adjustment (steps$batch_adjust with method in "combat_frozen", "location_scale", or "mean_center"). Batch labels come from batch (a vector) or batch_col (a column of X, removed from the predictors unless keep_batch_col = TRUE; a kept batch column is passed through unadjusted). Two further options:

    protect

    FALSE (default) or TRUE. When batch and outcome are associated in the training data (p < 0.01), a warning is issued either way, because both choices are biased: without protection, part of the outcome signal is removed as batch effect, so performance is underestimated; with protect = TRUE (and a non-survival y), batch effects are estimated net of the outcome, per feature, from z ~ batch + y, the role of ComBat's mod. That keeps the signal, but the estimated batch effects carry fitted outcome noise, which can bias cross-validated performance upward (Nygaard et al., 2016); in simulation with 80/20 confounding and no true signal, cross-validated AUC rose by about 0.03-0.10, more with more features. The default is the conservative choice. New rows need only their batch label. With protect = TRUE only batch locations are adjusted (no per-batch scaling), because rescaling would also rescale the protected outcome effect. Outcome effects are estimated from variation within batches only; outcome contrasts that do not vary within batches are not protected (with a warning). If every batch holds a single outcome class, only differences between batches of the same class are removed; if no class spans two batches, no adjustment is applied. Both cases warn.

    unseen

    What happens at transform() for rows whose batch was not seen in training, has a missing label, or when no batch labels are supplied: such rows are left unadjusted, because batch effects are known only for training batches. "warn" (default) warns, "error" stops, "grand_mean" accepts it silently. Under batch-blocked or study-held-out CV every test batch is unseen; fit_resample() then reports this once, not per fold.

    The "combat_frozen" method is a simplified empirical-Bayes location/scale adjustment in the spirit of ComBat, not a reimplementation of ComBat's priors.

  • Variance/IQR filtering. Thresholds are compared with the variance and IQR of the imputed training data on its original scale (before normalization), so var_thresh and iqr_thresh keep their meaning under z-score or robust scaling.

  • Feature selection (optional; t-test, lasso, PCA).

All statistics are estimated on the training data and re-used for new data.

References

Nygaard, V., Rødland, E. A. and Hovig, E. (2016). Methods that remove batch effects while retaining group differences may lead to exaggerated confidence in downstream analyses. Biostatistics, 17(1), 29-39.

See also

[predict_guard()]

Examples

x <- data.frame(a = c(1, 2, NA), b = c(3, 4, 5))
fit <- guard_fit(x, y = c(1, 2, 3),
                 steps = list(impute = list(method = "median")),
                 task = "gaussian")
fit$transform(x)
#>    a  b
#> 1 -1 -1
#> 2  1  0
#> 3  0  1
